title: API backpressure triage matrix and hotpaths (runbook draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for triaging API backpressure patterns we see in the platform: persistent request timeouts, client-visible 429s (rate-limited or backpressured), degraded streaming (stalls/partial chunks), and elevated 5xx/error rates. The intent is to give on-call engineers quick hypotheses, concrete probes, and low-risk mitigations to buy time while engineers investigate root cause.

Scope / assumptions:
- Applies to the Redwood hosted API and edge-proxied customer traffic (edge + runtime).
- Focus on production traffic (not dev/test).
- Target users: SRE on-call, incident commander, and engineers doing the first 1–2 hour triage.

Quick triage matrix (one-page mental model):
- Symptom: Timeouts (client HTTP TTFB > normal SLA, or streaming stalls)
  - Top hypotheses: 1) Upstream runtime overloaded (GPU pool saturated, long token latency), 2) Network egress/ingress congestion, 3) Slow external dependency (KV store, user metadata), 4) Garbage collection or memory pressure on workers.
  - Quick probes: check per-route p50/p95/p99 latency in dashboard, check GPU utilization and queue depth, check redis/metadata latency, check recent deploys.
  - Immediate mitigations: scale up replicas, enable smaller model fallback, activate per-route circuit-breaker to reject heavy requests, shift traffic to healthy region.

- Symptom: 429s spike (client receives 429s at higher-than-expected rate)
  - Top hypotheses: 1) Global rate limiter threshold hit (burst of legitimate traffic), 2) Backpressure from downstream (runtime returning 429 for queue capacity), 3) Misconfigured burst/bandwidth setting in edge envoy host.
  - Quick probes: review rate limiter metrics (tokens/sec, refill), check edge logs for limiter-origin tag, check if 429s show upstream=runtime or edge-proxy.
  - Immediate mitigations: temporarily bump rate limit token bucket for specific client / route, enable graceful fallback that returns a short synthetic response, or enable queueing mode (if supported) instead of hard reject.

- Symptom: Degraded streaming (partial chunks, long pauses between chunks)
  - Top hypotheses: 1) Runtime token generation stalling (KV cache thrash), 2) TCP/HTTP downstream buffering at edge or client, 3) Proxy-level flow control limiting chunk size.
  - Quick probes: tail streaming logs for chunk timestamps, compare server-side chunk emit times vs edge-to-client times, run curl with --no-buffer from edge to client to replicate.
  - Immediate mitigations: route to non-edge path (bypass CDN), temporarily lower streaming chunk size, or failover to non-streaming mode (short poll) for affected clients.

- Symptom: Elevated application 5xx rate (500/502/503)
  - Top hypotheses: 1) Recent deploy introduced NPE/availability bug, 2) dependent service outage (database, KVS), 3) autoscaler overshot/underscaled pool.
  - Quick probes: review deployment timeline (last 30m), check error logs grouped by exception signature, check third-party status pages.
  - Immediate mitigations: rollback last deploy for the service, route traffic to dedicated capacity or fallback model, or put a temporary static response for non-critical routes.

Checklist: first 15 minutes
- Announce incident in #sre-oncall and create a Jira incident (template below).
- Determine scope: percentage of requests failing vs total, affected routes, customers. Use metrics: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, active connections.
- Isolate origin: edge vs runtime vs backend (use origin tag in logs).
- Take a low-risk mitigation to buy time (rate-limit change, small scale-out, small rollback).

Key dashboards / queries (examples)
- Edge: edge.requests{status>=400} by origin, edge.latency.p95, envoy_rejects_total (labels: reason).
- Runtime: runtime.token_latency_ms{model,seq_len}, runtime.queue_depth, gpu_utilization{pool}.
- Storage: redis.latency_ms, postgres.active_connections, metadata_service_5xx.
- Streaming: stream.chunk_interval_ms{route}, stream.client_buffered_bytes.

Useful commands / playbook snippets
- Check pods by age and restart count (kubernetes):
  kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide --sort-by=.status.startTime
  kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n runtime | egrep "Restart|OOMKilled|Evicted"

- Scale runtime pool quickly (K8s HPA override):
  kubectl scale deployment runtime-pool-<pool> -n runtime --replicas=10
  NOTE: if using dedicated capacity, notify capacity team before changing slots.

- View Envoy reject logs (edge nodes):
  gcloud logging read "resource.type=gae_app AND textPayload:envoy" --limit 200 | grep "rate_limit" -n

- Toggle per-route circuit breaker (feature flag):
  /ops/feature-flags set route.circuitbreaker.<route> enabled=true --reason "oncall mitigation" --expires=2h

- Bump rate limiter (safest to target one client or route):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" \
    https://ops-api.internal/api/ratelimit/adjust \
    -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","client_id":"<client>","tokens_per_min":2000}'
  Log change in incident ticket.

Hypothesis-driven probes (examples)
- Hypothesis: runtime queue backlog causing timeouts.
  Probe: inspect runtime.queue_depth over last 10m and cross-check with gpu_utilization. If queue depth high but GPU idle low, risk of starvation at frontend.

- Hypothesis: rate-limiter on edge is rejecting after a config push.
  Probe: search deploys for edge-config in last 30m, check config hash on failing nodes and compare to healthy nodes.

- Hypothesis: downstream KVS is slow causing request timeouts.
  Probe: run p95 query latency against redis cluster, check instance restart events.

Non-blocking mitigations (fast, low risk)
- Increase autoscaler target by one step for affected pool.
- Pin route to known-good runtime model variant (lower capacity but faster).
- Add temporary 2-minute retry wrapper at edge for idempotent calls (avoid retries for streaming endpoints).

When to escalate to SE / oncall page duty:
- If mitigation does not reduce customer visible error rate by 50% within 20 minutes, escalate and assign SE owner.
- If the issue affects >5% of total requests or a single customer with revenue impact, escalate to incident commander and paging list.

Post-incident capture (notes to include in Jira ticket)
- Timeline of symptoms and actions (include dashboard snapshots).
- Root-cause hypothesis and what evidence supports/contradicts it.
- Hotfixes applied and why.
- Rollback/restore steps and permanent fix work items (RFCs/PRs).
- Lessons learned and follow-up runbook updates.

Incident ticket template (copy into JIRA when opening)
- Summary: "[INCIDENT] <short description> — API timeouts/429s/streaming"
- Impact: routes/customers affected, percent of traffic, user-visible effects
- Detection: alert name(s) and threshold triggered
- Timeline: actions taken with timestamps
- Mitigation/temporary changes: commands/flags toggled, who approved
- Owner and next steps: SWEs assigned, SRE follow-ups, postmortem owner

Notes-to-self / rough ideas (unordered)
- Consider a separate streaming circuit that keeps chunk throughput separate from initial response latency.
- We should add a per-model queue depth metric that is tagged by customer tier — helps identify noisy tenants.
- Create a small admin page to allow safe rate-limit bump for specific customers (with audit trail).
- Look into using TCP keepalive metrics to differentiate network pauses vs server stalls.

Open questions / TODOs in this draft:
- Exact alert thresholds for p95 latency vs p99 for streaming vs non-streaming routes.
- Ownership of the admin rate-limit tool (ops vs product infra).
- Can we add synthetic streaming checks that validate chunk cadence every 15s?

Appendix: quick reference links
- Dashboards: /dashboards/edge/latency /dashboards/runtime/pools /dashboards/streaming/chunks
- Slack channels: #sre-oncall, #infra-runtime, #edge-ops
- Playbooks: CONFLUENCE-API-RESILIENCE-OVERVIEW

---
This is a working doc. Add your test commands, findings, and failed hypotheses below as you triage. Keep this short, copy-paste friendly, and avoid long root-cause speculation in early minutes.

Notes: Marcus — 2026-02-28 (minor edits: added streaming chunk interval metric suggestion)
